periods.activity_title: Unlocking Friendship: Pre-Reading and Word Hunt

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.59): two words that come to mind about friendship.
Let us read (p.59): word-search grid — find eight friendship-related words.
Let us read (p.59): share the word for ‘friend’ in your own language.

homework.task_brief: Let us read (p.59-60): fill in blanks — partner, buddies, companion, classmates.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick paired exchange: each student shares two words they connect with friendship and listens to their partner’s words. Collect a few responses on the board to build a shared vocabulary cloud.

Students work individually on the word-search grid in “Let us read” (p.59), hunting for eight friendship-related words horizontally and vertically. Pairs then compare finds and explain what each word means.

Brief whole-class discussion: students share what word their home language uses for ‘friend’ and notice how many synonyms exist across languages. Teacher consolidates the board cloud and previews the narrative by reading the title aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Mario’s story centres on distinguishing true friends from mere acquaintances — the pre-reading vocabulary work primes students for that distinction. Students who are hesitant to share their home-language word should be gently encouraged; this is a low-stakes oral moment. The fill-in-blanks task (partner, buddies, companion, classmates) is set as homework so the vocabulary roots are reinforced after the word-hunt energy.

periods.activity_title: Reading Part I: Mario’s Boast and the Invisible Chair

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.61): mid-story pause — True/False, grandfather’s attic find, prediction questions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Part I of the narrative aloud (p.59–61) with students following in their textbooks. Pause at key moments — Mario’s boast about his friends, grandfather’s wager — to let students absorb the scene.

Students answer the “Let us discuss” checkpoint questions (p.61): the True/False about Mario’s pride and the short-answer question about what grandfather took from the attic. Pairs share answers before a whole-class check.

Oral prediction round: students respond to the two open questions — will Mario face challenges, and will the magic work? Teacher notes a few predictions on the board without confirming or denying them, sustaining narrative curiosity.

periods.teacher_notes: The grandfather’s wager over a fruit chaat is the story’s central conceit — ensure students understand the word ‘wager’ before moving on. The invisible chair is introduced here; allow a moment of genuine puzzlement before moving to predictions. Common misreading: students sometimes think grandfather is unkind — draw out the care behind the challenge.

periods.activity_title: Reading Part II: The Chair Test and True Friends Revealed

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.64): end-of-story True/False, fill-in-blank bet, matching characters to actions.
Let us think and reflect (p.64): fill-in words describing the chair, why it was tricky and special.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Part II of the narrative aloud (p.61–64) with students following. Guide attention to the scene where Mario falls repeatedly and the moment Guneet, Asma, and Deepa silently support him.

Students complete the “Let us discuss” end-of-story questions (p.64) individually: the True/False about Mario’s first attempt, the fill-in-blank about the bet, and the matching of characters to actions. Pairs check each other’s answers.

Class works through the passage-based questions in “Let us think and reflect” (p.64): two words describing the chair, why it was tricky to sit on, and why grandfather called it special. Teacher facilitates a brief whole-class share-out.

periods.teacher_notes: The emotional pivot of the story is the moment Mario looks around and sees his three friends holding him up — draw attention to the word ‘silently’ in the prose, as it carries the story’s moral weight. Students often confuse ‘tricky’ (invisible, so balance is impossible alone) with ‘magical’; the distinction matters for the passage questions. The remaining passage-analysis and extended-response questions are not taken up here.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading and Reflection: What Is a Friend for Life?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.64-65): passage 2 — fill-in technical problem, True/False, MCQ on Mario’s character.
Let us think and reflect (p.65): answer questions — the bet, first fall, how Mario found real friends.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.65): extended-response — is the magic chair test good? Friends for life meaning; other ways to find real friends.

time_bands.activity: Students read the second passage extract (p.64–65) independently and answer the three close-reading questions: fill-in-blank for Mario’s ‘technical problem’, the True/False about his friends being caring, and the MCQ on what his persistence shows. Pairs compare answers.

Whole-class guided discussion of the three short-answer questions in “Let us think and reflect” (p.65): what the bet was about, what happened on Mario’s first attempt, and how he found his real friends. Teacher uses the board to map character actions against the story’s moral.

Students begin the three extended-response questions (p.65) — whether the magic chair test was good, what ‘friends for life’ means personally, and other ways to find real friends — in writing. The three extended responses are completed as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read and discussed the full arc of Mario’s invisible chair test, students are now ready to move from recall to critical evaluation. The MCQ option ‘strong-willed’ is correct; watch for students choosing ‘hard-working’, which confuses persistent effort with the quality of refusing to give up in the face of social embarrassment. The three extended-response questions are substantive and require reflection time beyond the sitting.

periods.activity_title: Manu’s Story: Listening, Then Speaking About Friendship Qualities

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.68): fill in five blanks while listening to Manu talk about Monika.
Let us speak (p.68): pairs discuss four positive friend qualities from the list and give reasons.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the “Let us listen” transcript (Manu about Monika, p.73) aloud at a measured pace while students follow the five-blank fill-in task (p.68). The transcript is read a second time; students check and complete their answers. Whole-class verification follows.

Students move into pairs for “Let us speak” (p.68): each pair selects four positive qualities from the listed set — loving, honest, kind, caring, loyal, polite, respectful, team-worker, understanding — and uses the sentence-starter hints to explain their choices aloud. Teacher circulates, prompting quieter students with the provided frames.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript is self-contained (p.73); read it clearly and without rushing so students can isolate the five key words. The speaking task moves directly from listening to oral expression, keeping the theme of friendship qualities continuous. Encourage students who are hesitant to begin with the printed sentence starters before attempting free speech.

periods.activity_title: Writing a Message to a True Friend

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.69): choose correct words to complete Mario’s message to Guneet.
Let us write (p.69): write your own message to your best friend.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Mario’s three sample messages (p.69) aloud, then the class completes the guided fill-in task together — choosing the correct bracketed word at each blank in Mario’s message to Guneet. Teacher elicits reasons for each word choice to build awareness of tone.

Students plan and draft their own personal message to a best friend (p.69), drawing on the story’s language and the qualities discussed in the speaking activity. Teacher models the opening line on the board and then withdraws, allowing independent writing.

Students exchange messages with a partner for a quick peer-read: the partner notes one phrase they found warm or specific. Two or three students volunteer to read their message to the class. Teacher offers brief formative feedback on word choice and sincerity of expression.

periods.teacher_notes: The modelled message to Guneet shows students the register — warm, specific, and grateful — before they write independently. Common pitfall: students write very short, generic messages (‘you are my best friend, you are nice’); the board model should demonstrate specificity by naming a real act of care, as Mario does in the story. Both the guided and independent writing tasks are completed within this sitting.

periods.activity_title: Root Words and Suffixes: Building Words from the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.65): divide six words into root word and suffix in the table.
Let us learn (p.66): match root words to suffixes; form words and write sentences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the concept of root words and suffixes using ‘friendly’ (friend + ly) as the worked example from p.65. Students complete the table independently, dividing suddenly, talking, carrying, called, and showed into root and suffix. Pairs compare and the class checks together.

Students work through the suffix-matching task (p.66): pairing each root word (magic, care, celebrate, laugh, wonder, help, friend, courage) with a suitable suffix from the list, noting spelling changes, and writing a sentence using the formed word. Teacher circulates to address spelling-change queries (e.g., celebrate → celebration).

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently attach suffixes mechanically without noticing spelling changes — alert the class to the -e drop (celebrate → celebration) and the -y change (carry → carrying) before they begin the matching task. Both tasks draw exclusively on words present in the story, keeping the grammar work anchored to the text students have already read.

periods.activity_title: Adjectives in Action: Describing Mario and Building Phrases

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.66): write adjectives around the image of Mario to describe his character.
Let us learn (p.67): match adjectives to nouns; form phrases and write sentences.
Let us learn (p.67): complete the paragraph using adjective-noun pairings from the word box.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the story line ‘Mario, brave and determined, took the strange invisible chair’ (p.66) and asks students to identify the adjectives. Students then write adjectives around the Mario image in their textbook, drawing from the story and their own vocabulary. Class shares adjectives.

Students complete the adjective-noun matching table (p.67) — pairing brave, clever, tasty, heavy, slight, and true with nouns from Column B, forming phrases in Column C and sentences in Column D. Teacher points out that more than one combination is valid and models one example.

Students read the short paragraph frame (p.67) and fill in the seven blanks using the adjective-noun pairings from the word box. Partners swap books for a quick check. Teacher reads the completed paragraph aloud to confirm answers and discusses why each pairing fits.

periods.teacher_notes: The adjective focus is introduced through the story’s own language, ensuring grammar remains contextual rather than abstract. Students often default to only the adjectives printed in the story; prompt them to think of their own words when describing Mario. The paragraph-completion task at p.67 consolidates adjective-noun collocation in a narrative context.

periods.activity_title: FRIENDS Acrostic: A Creative Poem About My Friends

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.70): write an acrostic poem using the letters of FRIENDS.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.70): find and prepare to share a friendship story from your state or another country.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces acrostic poems by writing the word FRIENDS vertically on the board and composing one line collaboratively with the class. Discuss how each line should describe a quality or memory of a friend, using vivid words.

Students write their own FRIENDS acrostic poem (p.70) independently, filling each letter line with a description drawn from their experience of friendship. Teacher circulates, encouraging students to move beyond single adjectives and attempt a phrase or image for each letter.

Students volunteer to read their acrostic aloud. The class identifies the most vivid or surprising line in each poem and offers brief appreciative comments. Teacher notes outstanding phrases on the board as a shared gallery.

periods.teacher_notes: The acrostic task extends the story’s theme of friendship into personal creative expression. Students sometimes write single adjectives for each letter without elaborating; encourage a short phrase or an image (e.g., ‘R — Ready to laugh even on hard days’). The friendship-story research task is assigned as homework so students can gather responses before the final unit.

periods.activity_title: Friendship Across Ages: Interviewing and Presenting

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.70): interview people from four age groups about friendship; record, discuss, present findings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the interview-based project (p.70): students will compare how people of different ages understand friendship. Review the four age groups and the guiding question ‘What does friendship mean to you?’ Students plan two or three follow-up probes.

Small groups (3–4 students) pool responses they have gathered or recall from their own lives across the four age groups, record them in the table format, and discuss similarities and differences. Each group identifies one key theme and one surprising finding.

Groups present their key theme and surprising finding to the class in an unhurried round. Teacher consolidates recurring ideas on the board and leads a brief whole-class reflection on how the concept of friendship in the story connects to what real people across ages said.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored the story’s fable of invisible loyalty, students now ground the theme in lived perspectives across generations. Where students have not had opportunity to interview people formally, encourage them to draw on family members’ views recalled from conversation. The project’s value lies in the comparison and reflection, not in the completeness of the data table.

items.source_lo: Student reads a narrative text to retrieve information, make inferences, and evaluate character and theme using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Mario’s invisible chair test, grandfather’s wager, Guneet, Asma and Deepa as true friends.
items.item_stem:
Read the statements below about the events in the story ‘The Chair’ and mark each one True or False.
1. Mario’s grandfather challenged him to a bet of fruit chaat to prove a point about friendship.
2. Mario successfully sat on the invisible chair on his very first attempt at school.
3. Guneet, Asma, and Deepa silently moved behind Mario and held him up so he would not fall.
4. The classmates who did nothing but watch and laugh were revealed as Mario’s true friends.

options.text: Guneet, Asma, and Deepa silently moved behind Mario and held him up so he would not fall.
Mario successfully sat on the invisible chair on his very first attempt at school.
Mario’s grandfather challenged him to a bet of fruit chaat to prove a point about friendship.
The classmates who did nothing but watch and laugh were revealed as Mario’s true friends.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — grandfather wagered a fruit chaat that most of Mario’s supposed friends were merely companions, not true friends.
2. False — Mario fell repeatedly before finally being supported.
3. True — the three friends quietly positioned themselves behind him and held him up.
4. False — the laughing classmates were shown to be mere acquaintances, not true friends.

items.source_lo: Student reads a narrative text to retrieve information, make inferences, and evaluate character and theme using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Mario’s invisible chair test, grandfather’s wager, Guneet, Asma and Deepa as true friends.
items.item_stem: In the story, the grandfather uses an invisible chair to help Mario discover who his real friends are. What does the invisible chair represent as a metaphor for friendship? In your answer, refer to at least one specific moment from the story to support your thinking.

expected_elements: The chair represents the invisible tests every true friendship must pass.
Reference to the moment Mario falls and three friends silently support him.
Contrast between friends who help and classmates who only mock.
Idea that true friendship is revealed through action, not words.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a first-person account to identify specific details and understand how a supportive friendship develops using a spoken narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Manu’s account of Monika’s support when joining a new school; five key blanks.
items.item_stem:
Listen carefully to Manu’s account of joining a new school. Then answer: Which TWO actions did Monika take that made Manu feel comfortable in the new school?
A. She introduced Manu to other students and shared her notes.
B. She helped Manu with her homework every evening at home.
C. She guided Manu through the school and supported her.
D. She organised a welcome party so Manu could make friends quickly.

options.label: A
options.text: She introduced Manu to other students and shared her notes.

options.label: B
options.text: She helped Manu with her homework every evening at home.

options.label: C
options.text: She guided Manu through the school and supported her.

options.label: D
options.text: She organised a welcome party so Manu could make friends quickly.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Students who choose this import an assumption not in the transcript; Monika’s help was at school, not at home.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Students who choose this confuse a general notion of welcome with the specific, quiet support Monika gave.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a first-person account to identify specific details and understand how a supportive friendship develops using a spoken narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Manu’s account of Monika’s support when joining a new school; five key blanks.
items.item_stem: Manu says she is ‘really thankful’ to Monika. Based on what you heard in the account, explain in your own words how Monika’s support turned into a lasting friendship. Use at least two details from the account in your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Monika guided Manu when she first joined, introduced her to others, and shared her notes, making adjustment easier. Over time, the two experienced both difficult and happy moments together, and this shared experience deepened the support into a genuine, lasting friendship.

items.source_lo: Student expresses and justifies opinions about personal values in a paired conversation using spoken interaction as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Choosing four positive friend qualities from a given list and giving reasons using sentence-starter frames.
items.item_stem: In the story, Guneet, Asma, and Deepa show Mario what true friendship looks like. Think about the qualities of a good friend — such as being caring, loyal, honest, or understanding. Choose TWO qualities you believe are most important in a friend and describe, in a short talk (about one minute), what each quality means to you. Give an example from your own life or from the story to support each choice.

expected_elements: Names two qualities from the list with clear meaning.
Supports each choice with a personal or story-based example.
Uses complete sentences and audible, steady speech.
Gives a reason or consequence for why each quality matters.

items.source_lo: Student expresses and justifies opinions about personal values in a paired conversation using spoken interaction as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Choosing four positive friend qualities from a given list and giving reasons using sentence-starter frames.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are Mario, and a younger student at school asks you: ‘How do I know who my real friends are?’ Role-play this conversation with a partner. Mario should explain what he learned from the invisible chair experience, and the younger student should ask at least one follow-up question. You will each speak for about a minute.

expected_elements: Mario’s role draws on the story’s lesson about actions over words.
At least one specific reference to a friend quality discussed in class.
Younger student’s follow-up question is relevant and in character.
Speakers take turns and respond to each other, not just monologue.

items.source_lo: Student writes a personal message to a friend by selecting appropriate words and expressing specific gratitude using functional writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Mario’s message to Guneet; guided fill-in then independent message to own best friend.
items.item_stem: Asma was one of the three friends who silently supported Mario during the invisible chair test. Write a short thank-you note (4–5 sentences) from Mario to Asma. Your note must: mention a specific action Asma took, use a warm and sincere tone, and end with a phrase that shows why Asma’s friendship is valuable to Mario.

expected_elements: Names the specific act: silently moving behind Mario and holding him up.
Uses warm, sincere language appropriate to a personal message.
Closes with a phrase expressing lasting friendship or gratitude.
Writes in 4–5 complete sentences with correct punctuation.

items.source_lo: Student writes a personal message to a friend by selecting appropriate words and expressing specific gratitude using functional writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Mario’s message to Guneet; guided fill-in then independent message to own best friend.
items.item_stem: At the end of the story, Mario realises that true friends are those who care for you and would never take joy in your bad luck. Think about a time when a friend stood by you or helped you through something difficult. Write a personal message (one paragraph, 6–8 sentences) to that friend. Your message should: describe what happened in your own words, explain how their support made you feel, and say what their friendship means to you now.

expected_elements: Describes a specific personal event or moment of support.
Expresses emotional response to the friend’s act clearly.
Reflects on the lasting meaning of the friendship.
Uses warm, personal register in 6–8 complete sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: suddenly — sudden + ly, carrying — carry + ing, called — call + ed, showed — show + ed, friendly — friend + ly, talking — talk + ing

items.source_context: Root words and suffixes from the story (friendly, suddenly, talking); adjectives brave, clever, tasty, heavy, slight, true paired with nouns.
items.item_stem:
The story describes Mario as ‘brave and determined’. Choose ONE adjective from the list below and write TWO sentences about a character or object from ‘The Chair’ using that adjective. In your first sentence, pair the adjective with a noun from the story. In your second sentence, explain what that adjective tells the reader about the character or object.
Adjectives to choose from: clever, caring, slight, true.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Answers will vary. A strong response pairs the adjective with a story noun (e.g., ‘true friends’, ‘slight technical problem’, ‘clever grandfather’) and explains in the second sentence how the adjective adds meaning — for example: ‘The grandfather had a clever plan. This adjective shows the reader that grandfather’s test was carefully thought out, not just a trick.’

items.item_stem:
Write an acrostic poem using the word FRIENDS. Each line of your poem should describe a quality, action, or feeling connected to friendship, drawing on ideas from the story ‘The Chair’ or your own experience. Aim for a vivid phrase or image on each line, not just a single adjective.

F
R
I
E
N
D
S

expected_elements: All seven letters used with a phrase or image on each line.
At least two lines draw on story ideas (support, loyalty, care).
Language is vivid — phrases preferred over single adjectives.
Poem reads as a coherent, personal reflection on friendship.

items.source_lo: Student extends understanding of a theme through creative writing and cross-generational inquiry using hands-on and project tasks as the vehicle.
items.source_context: FRIENDS acrostic poem; interview project asking four age groups what friendship means.
items.item_stem: You have asked people from four age groups (12–19, 20–30, 31–49, 50+) what friendship means to them. Based on the responses you gathered, write a short report (two paragraphs) that: (a) describes ONE similarity and ONE difference you noticed across the age groups, and (b) explains, with a reason, how the ideas about friendship you found in ‘The Chair’ connect to the views shared by any one of your interviewees.

expected_elements: Clearly states one similarity and one difference across age groups.
Links interview findings to a specific idea from ‘The Chair’.
Report is organised in two coherent paragraphs.
Uses evidence from interview responses to support claims.
